correctness.rationale: The Binet pair for u=3+2sqrt2 yields the exact identity 2S_n(k)=k+B_k C_(2n+k+1). Consecutive differences equal 8B_k B_(2n+k+2). The stride-two subsequence has gcd 1 (k odd) or 6 (k even), by the order-two unimodular recurrence and parity residues. Thus the infinite GCD reduces to gcd(S_0,8B_k) or gcd(S_0,48B_k). For odd k, S0 and Bk odd and the identity gives gcd(k,Bk). For even k, odd primes not 3 follow from 2S0 congruent k mod Bk; prime 3 uses v3(Bk)>=v3(k)+1 and C_(k+1)=0 mod3, while prime 2 uses the doubling formula and mod4 congruences to obtain v2(S0)=v2(Bk)=v2(k). These complete prime valuation comparisons establish equality for every positive k, not just tested windows. Independently, 24 consecutive start positions for each k=1..110, exact sum identities and Python integer gcds all match; finite tests alone do not prove the infinite gcd.

originality.rationale: The strongest same-object primary source Mbirika--Schrader--Spilker (2023), Question 30, explicitly asks for the Lucas-balancing square GCD rather than giving the formula. Its earlier unsquared GCD formulas do not imply the square result. The generalized-Fibonacci square theorem has a different characteristic recurrence. Resultary and indexed sequence searches found no stronger theorem in this precise family. An important precision is that gcd(k,Bk) remains a gcd of a sequence term with its index, and the same source Question 31 warns such forms need not be a completely simplified closed form; originality attaches to the equality/reduction, not an unstated gcd-free factorization. Later/unindexed dominating results remain possible.
residual_risks: The answer gcd(k,Bk) remains a computational gcd and does not solve the separate prime-factor/rank-of-apparition simplification problem in Question 31; do not overstate the result as gcd-free closed form.
The underlying sum and difference identities are elementary consequences of Binet formulas; an unindexed general Lucas square-GCD theorem could cover the equality.
The 2023 paper gives related squared-GCD observations, so only the all-k exact new equivalence is credited.

value.rationale: The squared-sum Lucas-balancing GCD is singled out as an unsolved natural parameter family in Mbirika--Schrader--Spilker (2023) Question 30. A uniform exact reduction to gcd(k,Bk) replaces an infinite sliding-window GCD and isolates nontrivial 2-adic and 3-adic cancellations. The invariant is intrinsically natural and useful for later entry-point analysis even though the resulting gcd(k,Bk) is not itself a completely simplified prime-factor closed form (as their Question 31 explicitly notes). This mathematical usefulness does not require resolving all other Q30 families.

limitations: Only the squared-window Lucas-balancing C sequence; other three Question 30 square-GCD families remain open in this finding.
The right side gcd(k,Bk) is exact but not a gcd-free explicit formula, in light of the motivating paper Question 31.
Possible implicit/general Lucas recurrence formula remains a historical-priority risk.
